chartContributions.notes: Spelled Bellinghausen on both charts. The transliteration is the chart's, not ours, and is kept as the chart gives it.
A commercial voyage compiled into an Admiralty chart, which is the point at which sealing knowledge becomes hydrographic knowledge.
The oldest voyage on both sheets, and the only one that predates the idea of an Antarctic continent as a survey target.
One of the two additions that distinguish the 1910 issue from its 1874 predecessor.

The chart dates d'Urville 1839 although the Adelie coast sighting is generally dated January 1840. A chart's own dating is evidence about the chart, and is recorded as the chart gives it rather than corrected silently.
A magnetic and pendulum survey, present on the chart for its ice observations rather than for any discovery.
The other addition, and the reason the 1910 sheet exists at all.
The last voyage on the 1874 sheet, and the survey the earlier sightings are reconciled against.

Not a voyage but a set of papers on icebergs, credited in the 1874 title and absent from the 1910 one. A compilation that cites an analysis rather than an observation is exactly the distinction between surveyed and reconciled geography, and it is the one contribution here that never went south.
The exceptional ice year, compiled alongside ordinary ones without a note that it was exceptional. That flattening is itself part of what Act VII should show.
Same dating question as d'Urville. Wilkes appears on a chart that also carries Ross, whose voyage contradicted part of what Wilkes charted.

coastline.notes: Confirmed by the Australasian expedition seventy years later, which is also why Mawson is a Act VII candidate on cartographic rather than heroic grounds.
A hundred years between the claim and any reliable confirmation date, and the confirmation date recorded here is itself approximate. That interval is the finding, not a defect in the row.

Filed as modified rather than confirmed because an ice front is not a coastline and does not stay where it was charted. A chronology that treated it as confirmed coast would be wrong in a way no later survey could correct.
No geometry: what was seen and where is the contested question, and drawing a segment would answer it. The chronology fields carry what is known, which is a claimed date and nothing confirmed.
The only segment here filed as a direct observation, and the one whose four dates are all present. It is the shape a well-evidenced coast has, and the others are measured against it.

coastline.displayName: The coast charted as Wilkes Land
coastline.notes: `first_observed_date` is deliberately empty while `first_claimed_date` is not. That gap between claiming and observing is the whole of the Wilkes problem, and a schema that forced one date would hide it.

phases.notes: Sequence 0 because it never happened. It is the intention against which every later phase is read, and it is held as a separate entity so that the plan and the experience can never be merged into one route.

phases.displayName: South Georgia into the Weddell Sea
phases.notes: The only phase in which the ship goes where it is steered.
The hinge of the act. Recorded as 19 January; sources seen during compilation also give 18 January, and that disagreement is logged as ant-gap-besetment-date rather than resolved by choosing.
Nine months in which the ship's position changes continuously and its crew steer nothing. The `under_own_power` field exists for this row: a drift must never read as a voyage.
Abandonment and sinking are twenty-five days apart and are two events, not one.
The people continue to move geographically after the ship is gone, which is the cleanest statement of the act's question.
A second navigation problem with different constraints: few sights, a moving platform and no margin for a longitude error.
Included because it is navigation without a chart, which is the last variation the act has to offer.

priorityClaims.contestedBy: Whether an ice front counts as a sighting of land
priorityClaims.notes: The strongest case if an ice front observed from close inshore counts, and no case at all if the definition requires rock. That is a definitional question, not an evidential one, and the row records which definition it answers rather than whether it wins. Dependence on Debenham's 1945 translation is declared rather than the Russian original consulted (ant-gap-bellingshausen-translation): the wording this row and its contest rest on is Debenham's English, and an upgrade to the Russian text is future work, not a precondition for holding this row at contested.

priorityClaims.contestedBy: Whether what was seen was the mainland peninsula or islands off it
priorityClaims.notes: Three days after Bellingshausen and against a different definition, which is why comparing the two dates settles nothing on its own.

priorityClaims.contestedBy: Overlap in time and place with the United States squadron
priorityClaims.notes: Three expeditions on overlapping coast in one season is the best case Act V has, and the essay currently has one of the three charts located.

priorityClaims.contestedBy: A sealing log as the record, and a date ten months later than the other two
priorityClaims.notes: The weakest of the three on date alone, and the one whose evidence is a commercial document rather than a naval one. Both facts are about the archive, not about what was seen.

priorityClaims.assertedBy: Argument from the incentives of the trade
priorityClaims.notes: Recorded as a row with no date and no observation, which is the honest shape of an argument from silence. It exists so the contest cannot be presented as a closed field of three.

priorityClaims.contestedBy: Ross sailing across positions charted as land
priorityClaims.notes: A claim to continental extent rather than to a first sighting, which is a different contest and is filed as one. Parts of it survived and parts did not.

records.notes: A sub-Antarctic phantom rather than a continental one, kept because it is the clearest case of the pattern the reusable methodology is for: report, repetition, search, removal. records.title: Dougherty Island
records.whatWasReported: An island reported in the far South Pacific, with a described position, subsequently repeated on charts and searched for by later vessels.
records.whyPlausible: A single reported position in an ocean nobody crossed often, in an era when a chart had no way to record that a feature rested on one unconfirmed report.

records.title: Emerald Island
records.whatWasReported: An island reported south of New Zealand and carried on charts for over a century.
records.whyPlausible: The southern ocean between Australasia and the ice was crossed rarely and charted from scattered reports, so a single sighting had little against it.

records.title: Frisquemore
records.whatWasReported: A country said to have been discovered in 1650 by two French captains of Saint Malo, Lozieres and Courtais, who placed it on the confines of Lapland and of the Samoyeds and divided it into twelve provinces: Frisquemorenna, Sainctyonide, Taupierie, Tillitie, Brossieride, Pichotelanne, Clauzellique, Gadrettona, Sovillacia, Godefrira, Touronnide and Fresnence. The relation was printed at Paris in 1662.
records.whyPlausible: Two named captains from a real port, a date, twelve named provinces and a printed relation are the furniture of a true account. The ground it claimed was the far north, where nobody in Paris was in a position to check it.

records.title: The Isle of Pines
records.whatWasReported: An island to the south of Africa. In Coronelli's telling some Englishmen sent four vessels in 1589, in the reign of Queen Elizabeth, to establish the East India trade; one was wrecked on the unknown coasts of the south and none survived but a young man named Giorgio Pines and four women, one of them a Moor. A Flemish ship thrown to the island by bad weather in 1667 found the five multiplied to ten or twelve thousand, speaking English, holding a written descent left by Pines at his death aged eighty; a descendant gave it to the Fleming to keep the memory, and it was printed at Roano in 1668.
records.whyPlausible: The southern coasts were genuinely unknown and ships genuinely disappeared on the East India run, so the premise cost nothing to believe. The account also came with the apparatus of proof: a dated wreck, a named survivor, a second independent ship, a document, and a printing.

records.notes: The programme's strongest ghost case after Wilkes, and the one that connects Act VI directly to Act VIII: Endurance drifted through the water Morrell had charted as land. records.title: New South Greenland
records.whatWasReported: An extensive coast reported in the Weddell Sea, running south from around 62 degrees south, described with landmarks and soundings.
records.whyPlausible: Morrell was sailing in the same exceptional ice year that let Weddell reach an extraordinary latitude, in a sea that was demonstrably open that season and closed in most others. A coast reported from there in 1823 was not absurd on its face.

records.title: The Parry Mountains
records.whatWasReported: A range reported to the south of the Ross Sea coast and named after Ross's former commander.
records.whyPlausible: Ross was an experienced observer working in clear polar air, where distance and elevation are notoriously hard to judge and where a far snowfield can read as a nearer range.

records.claimant: Anonymous; the history printed at Paris by Claudio Barbin in 1677
records.laterEvidence: Coronelli rules the history suspect in 1691 and gives his grounds: no author's name is attached; the circumstances described are paradoxical; and the same history dates the discovery to 1427, so two and a half centuries would have passed without a word of it reaching European countries. He adds an anachronism, that a great priest of the Sun could not have ruled in Persia in that century, Persia having been under Islamic law since Mohammed's lifetime.
records.notes: The first of the two invented countries Coronelli recounts at length before rejecting them, and the fullest rejection on the page: he argues from the missing author, the internal implausibility, the silence of two and a half centuries and a dated anachronism. records.title: The land of the Sevarambi
records.whatWasReported: A peopled part of the Terra Australe lying opposite Persia. Persian pilots bound for the East Indies were carried there by winds and sea storms and forced to land; word of the discovery reached Sevaris, high priest of the Sun, who went with armed ships to take possession, was made master of the country, and built a city he named Sevarinde with a temple to the Sun. The two peoples he found, the Prestarambi and the Strucarambi, were called Sevarambi after him. Coronelli takes the account from a history printed at Paris by Claudio Barbin in 1677.
records.whyPlausible: A southern continent opposite Persia was ordinary geography in 1677, and the report arrived in the shape a true discovery took: a storm-driven landfall, a return to a known port, and a printed relation. Coronelli himself calls the things told of them close to dreamed and touching on the incredible, which is a judgement about the contents and not about the form.

records.title: Terra de' Papagalli
records.whatWasReported: A land placed on the charts next to the Terra di Vista, south of the Cape of Good Hope. Some report, Coronelli writes, that a Frenchman called Gonneville arrived there in 1504 and was received by a petty king named Arosca, and that after several months he took home to Normandy some people of that country, among them Essomerice Meriu, the son of one of those kings.
records.whyPlausible: Alone in this list the story has a named traveller, a named host and named people carried back to Normandy, where they could in principle have been met. That is the strongest form a report of an unvisited land can take, and it is the form a chart has no way to distinguish from a true one.

records.claimant: Not named by Coronelli, who attributes it to 'qualche Carta Geografica'
records.laterEvidence: Coronelli states no verdict on this name in the sentence that introduces it. The paragraph that follows opens 'Queste Favole si possono aggiungere', these fables may be added to those of the City of Tartar and the rest, which sweeps the cape and the Terra de' Papagalli into the fables retrospectively.
records.notes: The weakest reading on the page, and marked as such rather than levelled up to match its neighbours. The verdict reaches this name by the following paragraph's pickup of 'Queste Favole' and not by a sentence of its own, so 'disproved' rests on Coronelli's sentence order. It is also the only feature here he places by latitude, 42 degrees south, which is exactly why it carries no geometry: drawing a cape for a rejected coast from one figure and no longitude would repeat the original error in our own voice. later_status is 'disproved' with ant-src-coronelli-atlante-veneto named as the source of the disproof, which records that the verdict is Coronelli's in 1691 and not ours. current_scholarly_status stays 'unresolved' because this dataset holds no modern authority on the feature, and inheriting a seventeenth-century judgement as a present-day one is the error the two fields exist to keep apart. Confidence raised from low to medium 2026-08-27, when the remaining four leaves were read: all seven printed pages of the essay have now been examined, and the southern discourse proves to run only from mid-p. 75 to p. 76, so this verdict rests on an argument read in full rather than on three pages of seven. It stays below high because the record remains a single seventeenth-century witness and no modern authority on the feature has been consulted.
records.sourceLocator: Atlante Veneto Tomo I, 'Terre Polari, Artiche, ed Antartiche', printed page 76 (Rumsey 12186.107)
records.title: Terra di Vista
records.whatWasReported: A coast of the Terra Australe described on some geographical charts to the south of the Cape of Good Hope, from which a cape runs out at 42 degrees of southern latitude. The cape is given the name Terra di Vista, and the Terra de' Papagalli is placed next to it. Coronelli reports no voyage, no discoverer and no date for it.
records.whyPlausible: It was on the charts, which in 1691 was a form of authority in itself, and it stood in the stretch of the southern ocean where a continental coast was expected rather than merely possible. A latitude is attached to it, which is what a real observation would have left behind.

records.laterEvidence: Later vessels sailed across positions charted as land.
records.notes: Deliberately carries no geometry. Which segment, at what position, on which sheet is unknown (ant-gap-wilkes-sheets), and drawing a line for a disproof we cannot locate would repeat the original error in our own voice. current_scholarly_status stays unresolved because much of Wilkes's coast was correct.
records.title: Coast charted by Wilkes and later sailed through (segment to be identified)
records.whatWasReported: Continuous southern coast observed and charted over an extended run of longitude.
records.whyPlausible: A long coast seen repeatedly over many days from a squadron of ships, in conditions where distant ice and distant land are hard to tell apart.
